inventory.name: Disconnect open WebSocket connections on BFCache entry and fire close event

syntax.rationale: The feature is a browser behavior change adding no new Web API or grammar surface ('Status: Browser behavior change (no new API)', #at-a-glance; the ChromeStatus record reports feature_type 'No developer-visible change'), so the declaration surface this page documents is the event and state contract in #what-changes: open WebSocket connections close on cache entry, the close event is fired on each socket, the document enters BFCache, and pageshow fires with event.persisted === true upon restore. The fragment contains semantic <code> tags for each participating interface and event token.

inputs.rationale: #reconnect-example documents the input surfaces the application consumes on BFCache transition: the WebSocket constructor URL string ('wss://example.com/live') and the window pageshow event whose persisted input property (event.persisted === true) signals that the page was restored from BFCache rather than loaded anew. No new input arguments or dictionaries are introduced.

outputs.rationale: #what-changes documents the observable output events: on BFCache entry Chrome closes open WebSocket connections and dispatches the 'close' event on each socket, storing the page in the cache; on BFCache restore, the 'pageshow' event is fired on window with event.persisted === true. No new return value or object is returned directly to synchronous caller code.

errors.rationale: The behavior change introduces no new exception or DOMException types. Closing the socket on cache entry triggers normal WebSocket disconnection handling (firing close and error events), and compatibility notes documents that legacy applications failing to handle close will stall after restore rather than throw an exception. The feature defines no custom error surface.

context.rationale: #at-a-glance defines the execution and exposure context: shipped in Chrome 149 for desktop and Android as a browser behavior change with no feature flag, governed by WHATWG HTML PR #12349 and verified by WPT tests.

lifecycle.rationale: #what-changes documents the lifecycle state transitions: when the document navigates away and qualifies for BFCache entry, open WebSocket connections are closed and their close events fire; while cached, execution is suspended in memory; on navigation restore, window fires pageshow with persisted: true, signaling the app to reconnect.

examples.rationale: #reconnect-example provides a complete runnable code example showing how to initialize a WebSocket connection, register a close event handler to schedule reconnection, and listen for the window pageshow event checking event.persisted and ws.readyState to re-establish connections upon BFCache restoration.

compatibility.rationale: #browser-support provides a tabular browser compatibility matrix listing Chrome 149 (desktop and Android) and Edge 149, alongside Firefox and Safari notes regarding BFCache support and differing WebSocket handling, citing ChromeStatus feature 5068439115923456.

securityPrivacy.rationale: The behavior change introduces no new permission, origin trial, credential exposure, or cross-origin security boundary. Sockets are closed before caching to prevent background network activity while a page is frozen in memory, and server-side sessions see a standard close identical to a client network drop.

It\'s therefore good practice to close the connection when the user has finished with the page.' (B) Safari browser view divergence: this page's browser support table states 'WebSocket behaviour may differ — check WebKit release notes' for Safari, while ChromeStatus feature 5068439115923456 records Safari as 'Shipped/Shipping' (val 1, citing WebKit standards-positions issue 648 where WebKit notes it already closes WebSocket connections on page cache entry). Neither side is adjudicated here; drafted disclosure paragraphs and pin entries are reported for the implementer.
